Lindsey Graham: Death of a Useful Villain

Lindsey Graham dies not on some mythical front line he funded, but after another sanctions victory lap in Kyiv and a torn artery in Washington. 

For Russia, he was not a propaganda invention but the finished product. He built his brand on treating Russia as an enemy to punish, not contain, boasting that his bills could “break the back” of the Russian economy and pushing to label Russia a state sponsor of terrorism. 

He openly floated the idea that someone in Moscow should “eliminate” Putin, forcing even Washington to clarify it does not endorse assassinating foreign leaders, and he raged at allies and his own administration for not hitting Russia hard enough.

In Ukraine he translated that hostility into open satisfaction at Russian losses. In Kyiv in 2023 he called U.S. aid “the best money we’ve ever spent” and, in the same sitting, observed with evident approval that “the Russians are dying.” 

He presented dead Russian soldiers and strangled Russian trade as proof America was finally using its power “correctly.”

His death is politically convenient. In Washington and Brussels, he is instantly canonized as the “lion” of the anti‑Kremlin cause whose crusade must now be completed by passing his next sanctions bill and weapons package. 

In Moscow’s media, no embellishment is needed: his own words, his own legislation, and his sudden collapse after a Kyiv trip are enough to sell him as the textbook Russophobe who spent years cheering Russian pain and then met his own.

Graham’s career was one long push to escalate a regional war into a permanent global confrontation, via sanctions, arms, and secondary punishment for anyone still dealing with Moscow. 

Now that he is gone, the same machine keeps grinding — in DC, invoked as a martyr whose “legacy” demands more pressure; in Russia, as proof that Russophobia is cursed; everywhere else, as a reminder that the loudest apostles of “freedom” almost never die in the wars they help ignite.

risk that lives on every account, every day, in every

🖥 Pakistani analyst: US chief violator of Islamabad memorandum, responsible for delay in talks

📌 Islamabad, IRNA – A senior Pakistani political analyst and journalist said Tuesday that the United States is the principal violator of the Islamabad memorandum of understanding and bears responsibility for delaying negotiations with Iran, criticizing Washington’s belligerent conduct toward Tehran.

Speaking on Pakistan’s Dunya News, Mazhar Abbas said the United States did not even wait out the 60-day window set by the Islamabad memorandum before beginning what he called provocative actions, in reference to recent US aggression against Iranian cities.
​
He said challenging Iran’s survival is the central agenda of the United States and Israeli regime, adding that neither side has genuinely sought to resolve the issues through recognized international channels.
​
The analyst said the core dispute is not the Strait of Hormuz but implementation of the terms of the Islamabad memorandum, under which the other side was to enter talks with Iran within 60 days of signing.
​
He said Washington violated that timeline and has since caused delays in negotiations with the Islamic Republic of Iran.
​
“Donald Trump is pretending to be the victim and using it as a winning card,” Abbas said, adding that Trump took no action to stop Israeli aggression against Lebanon.
​
He said no side other than Iran has shown a constructive and reasonable approach in the talks, while the Iranian people want assurances that their rights will not be trampled by the other side.
​
Separately, Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement Sunday that it was closely following developments in the region and expressed deep concern, calling on all parties to exercise maximum restraint and take immediate steps to honor their commitments under the Islamabad memorandum.
​
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei, addressing an IRNA question at a press briefing the previous day, said the Islamic Republic of Iran has never been the initiator of any violation of commitments.
​
He said Iran adheres to the principle of “commitment for commitment” and will continue to honor its obligations as long as the other side does the same, but will halt implementation of its own commitments if the United States continues violating its obligations.
